Hodges-Lehmann Estimator of Location

Source: R/hodgesLehmann.R
hodgesLehmann.Rd

Function to compute the Hodges-Lehmann estimator of location in the one and two sample case following a clever fast algorithm by John Monahan (1984).

Usage

hodgesLehmann(
  x,
  y = NULL,
  conf.level = NA,
  sides = c("two.sided", "left", "right"),
  method = c("exact", "boot"),
  na.rm = FALSE,
  ...
)

Arguments

x

numeric vector

y

optional numeric vector

conf.level

confidence level of the interval. If set to NA (the default), only the point estimate is returned. One-sided intervals require conf.level > 0.5.

sides

character string specifying the sidedness of the confidence interval (one of "two.sided" (default), "left" or "right"). See ConfidenceIntervals().

method

interval method: "exact" (default), the distribution-free interval obtained by inverting the Wilcoxon signed-rank (one-sample) or rank-sum (two-sample) test; or "boot", a bootstrap interval (one-sample only). Ignored without conf.level.

na.rm

logical; if TRUE, missing values are removed from x and y separately before the computation

...

additional arguments for method = "boot" (R, type, parallel, ncpus); an error with method = "exact". type = "stud" is not available: the bootstrap statistic carries no variance estimate per resample.

Value

if conf.level = NA, a numeric scalar. Otherwise a named numeric vector with elements:

est

point estimate of the Hodges-Lehmann location

lci

lower confidence interval bound

uci

upper confidence interval bound

Details

The Hodges-Lehmann estimator is the median of the combined data points and Walsh averages.

It is the same as the pseudo median returned as a by-product of wilcox.test() (which however does not calculate correctly as soon as ties are present).

Note that in the two-sample case the estimator for the difference in location parameters does not estimate the difference in medians (a common misconception) but rather the median of the difference between a sample from x and a sample from y.

sides names the side on which the finite bound lies: "left" yields \([lci, \infty)\), "right" yields \((-\infty, uci]\). The estimator is unbounded, so the open side is reported as \(\pm\infty\).

Missing values. NA and NaN are treated alike. With na.rm = FALSE, a missing value in x or y yields NA - a scalar, or c(est = NA, lci = NA, uci = NA) when an interval was requested. With na.rm = TRUE the missing values are removed from each sample separately; x and y are independent samples, not pairs. An empty sample, given or left over after the removal, yields NA as well. Invalid arguments are an error even when data are missing.

Infinite values are ordinary order statistics. NaN is returned when the median is undefined: if a pair yields Inf - Inf (-Inf and Inf both in x in the one-sample case, the same infinity in x and y in the two-sample case), or if the two middle order statistics are -Inf and Inf.

Exact interval. With method = "exact" the interval inverts the Wilcoxon signed-rank (one-sample) resp. rank-sum (two-sample) test (Bauer 1972). Its bounds are Walsh averages resp. differences x[i] - y[j], selected by Monahan's partitioning instead of sorting all \(O(n^2)\) values, so large samples are no problem.

  • Samples below 50 (both below 50 in the two-sample case) use the exact null distribution: the classic one without ties, the conditional (permutation) distribution given the midranks with ties.

  • Larger samples use the normal approximation with continuity and tie correction.

The results agree with wilcox.test(exact = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) (R >= 4.6.0) in the two-sample case and in the one-sample case without ties. With ties, wilcox.test() (R 4.6.1) takes the lower one-sample bound from \(P(V > v)\) instead of \(P(V \ge v)\), one rank too narrow, with coverage below the nominal level; hodgesLehmann() uses \(P(V \ge v)\). In the large-sample case wilcox.test() interpolates between Walsh averages with uniroot(), hodgesLehmann() returns the order statistics that bound the inverted test. If the requested level is not attainable (very small samples, e.g. \(n \le 5\) at 95\

Bootstrap interval. If all bootstrap replicates coincide (e.g. constant data), the interval collapses to lci = uci = est. With a single observation, or when the replicates are not all finite, no interval can be formed: lci and uci are NA with a warning.

x and y are not modified.

Note

C++ port of Monahan's algorithm by Cyril Flurin Moser

Random number generation

Only method = "boot" uses R's random number generator; call base::set.seed() beforehand for reproducible intervals. The point estimate and the exact interval are deterministic: the compiled routine picks its pivots from a local generator and does not touch R's stream.

References

Hodges, J. L., Lehmann, E. L. (1963). Estimates of location based on rank tests. The Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 34(2), 598–611. doi:10.1214/aoms/1177704172

Monahan, J. F. (1984). Algorithm 616: Fast computation of the Hodges-Lehmann location estimator. ACM Transactions on Mathematical Software, 10(3), 265–270. doi:10.1145/1271.319414 . Original code: https://www4.stat.ncsu.edu/~monahan/jul10/

Bauer, D. F. (1972). Constructing confidence sets using rank statistics. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 67(339), 687–690. doi:10.1080/01621459.1972.10481279

Efron, B. (1987). Better bootstrap confidence intervals. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 82(397), 171–185. doi:10.1080/01621459.1987.10478410

Davison, A. C., Hinkley, D. V. (1997). Bootstrap Methods and Their Application. Cambridge University Press.

See also

stats::wilcox.test()

Other location: gmean(), hmean(), huberM(), meanX(), medianX(), modeX(), tukeyBiweight()

Examples

x <- c(1.83, 0.50, 1.62, 2.48, 1.68, 1.88, 1.55, 3.06, 1.30)
hodgesLehmann(x)
#> [1] 1.725

# the input is left alone
v <- c(3, 1, 2)
hodgesLehmann(v)
#> [1] 2
v
#> [1] 3 1 2

# two-sample: median of the pairwise differences, NOT the difference
# of the medians
y <- c(0.878, 0.647, 0.598, 2.05, 1.06, 1.29, 1.06, 3.14, 1.29)
hodgesLehmann(x, y)
#> [1] 0.56

# missing values: NA, or removed per sample with na.rm
hodgesLehmann(c(x, NA), y)
#> [1] NA
hodgesLehmann(c(x, NA), y[-1], na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] 0.54

# distribution-free interval, one- and two-sample
hodgesLehmann(x, conf.level = 0.95)
#>   est   lci   uci 
#> 1.725 1.165 2.370 
hodgesLehmann(x, y, conf.level = 0.95)
#>    est    lci    uci 
#>  0.560 -0.220  1.082 
hodgesLehmann(x, conf.level = 0.95, sides = "left")
#>   est   lci   uci 
#> 1.725 1.425   Inf 

# bootstrap interval (one-sample)
set.seed(1)
hodgesLehmann(x, conf.level = 0.95, method = "boot", R = 999)
#>      est      lci      uci 
#> 1.725000 1.425000 2.211442
